result: A survey of 365 new PIs appointed in the UK between 2012-2018 was conducted, with respondents predominantly from life sciences (83%), male (57%), UK nationals (51%), and white (84%).
evaluation: The demographic characteristics are consistently reported across multiple claims with specific percentages and sample sizes. The data is presented clearly in both text and figures, providing a comprehensive demographic profile of the survey respondents.

result: New PIs had an average of seven years of postdoctoral experience before independence, with the majority in their mid-thirties when appointed. This duration likely reflects historical fellowship eligibility restrictions.
evaluation: Claims C6 and C132 provide specific data (7 years average, 51% between 5-7 years), while C130 confirms the resulting age distribution. Claim C7 offers a reasonable speculative explanation for the observed pattern, though it is explicitly marked as speculation.

result: Half of respondents had dependents, with female investigators more likely to have dependents and longer career breaks (10 months vs 5 months for men). Nearly all respondents (361/365) worked full-time despite family responsibilities.
evaluation: Multiple claims provide consistent data on family status, career breaks, and work patterns. The specific numbers and percentages are clearly stated and supported by figure references. The temporal pattern showing recent female appointees less likely to have dependents adds nuance.

result: International mobility is common among new PIs, with 67% undertaking at least one international move during their career, and 78% moving (including within UK) to take up their position. Only 27% spent their entire career in the UK.
evaluation: The claims provide consistent percentages about mobility patterns, supported by Figure 2. The data clearly shows the prevalence of international experience and movement in academic career progression.

result: While over 50% of respondents were optimistic about their future, significant dissatisfaction exists regarding space/facilities (24% dissatisfied) and work-life balance (33% dissatisfied). Having dependents did not affect optimism scores.
evaluation: The claims provide specific percentages for satisfaction across multiple domains, with clear distinctions between satisfied and dissatisfied groups. The finding that dependents don't affect optimism is explicitly stated and supported by figure references.

result: Two main career paths exist for new PIs in the UK: 41% were appointed as lecturers and 59% as research fellows. Russell Group universities accounted for 70-75% of respondents, predominantly hiring research fellows, while non-Russell Group institutions primarily hired lecturers.
evaluation: The claims consistently describe the two career paths with specific percentages and institutional distributions. The data is well-supported by figures and provides clear evidence of the structural differences between institution types.

result: 38% of new PIs were required to secure major grants or fellowships before taking up their position, with this requirement much more common for research fellows (52%) than lecturers (11%). Some research fellows secured over £500,000 before starting.
evaluation: The claims provide consistent percentages showing the differential funding requirements between career paths. The data clearly demonstrates that research fellows face substantially higher pre-appointment funding requirements than lecturers.

result: Male PIs secured significantly more grant funding than female PIs, with men more likely to secure funding exceeding £1m (p=0.025) and women receiving significantly fewer grants (p=0.039). Male PIs appear better able to gain momentum through continued grant success.
evaluation: The claims provide specific statistical evidence (p-values) for gender differences in grant success. The data shows both the number of grants and total funding amounts differ significantly by gender, with consistent patterns across multiple measures.

result: Female PIs were paid £3,000-5,000 less per year than male PIs (women averaged £31k vs men £45.6k in start-up funds), with women more likely to be appointed at lower grades. This grade difference will impact career progression rates.
evaluation: Multiple claims provide consistent evidence of gender pay gaps in both starting salaries and start-up funding, with specific monetary amounts. The appointment to lower grades for women is documented with figure support, and the inference about career progression impact is reasonable.

result: 57% of research fellows were expected to teach despite protected research time, with nearly 40% having >10 contact hours/year and 10-15% having >40 hours/year. Women had higher teaching loads than men in both lecturer and fellow positions.
evaluation: The claims provide specific percentages for teaching expectations across career paths and genders. The data clearly shows that research fellows face substantial teaching loads despite their positions being designated for research, with gender disparities evident.

result: Female PIs have higher teaching and administration loads than male PIs, which may contribute to their reduced grant success and smaller lab sizes. This could result from efforts to ensure gender balance on committees given fewer female PIs overall.
evaluation: Claims C46, C47, and C91 provide clear data on gender differences in workload. Claims C48, C111, and C115 offer reasonable inferences about the causes and consequences of these differences, though these are explicitly speculative.

result: Almost 25% of new PIs reported having no mentorship, with female PIs without mentors being the least optimistic about career progression. While 97% of lecturers had annual reviews, 18% of externally funded fellows did not.
evaluation: The claims provide specific percentages for mentorship and review processes, with clear evidence that lack of mentorship particularly affects female PIs' optimism. The differential support structures between lecturers and fellows are well-documented.

result: Most lecturers (88%) received start-up funds of £20-60K from their university, but male PIs received an average of £14.6K more than female PIs (£45.6k vs £31k).
evaluation: The claims provide consistent data on start-up funding with specific amounts and percentages. The gender gap in start-up funding is clearly documented with precise figures from both text and figure captions.

result: 70% of research fellows lacked proleptic appointments, and 58% were unaware of requirements for permanent positions. Despite supporting their own salaries and bringing in large grants, these fellows lack job security and can be made redundant with little consequence.
evaluation: The claims provide specific percentages documenting the precarious employment situation of research fellows. The paradox of high-performing researchers lacking job security is well-articulated, though the recommendation to funders (C129) is an inference.

result: While 80% of respondents had PhD students, both lecturers and fellows reported recruitment difficulties. Research fellows were more likely to have postdocs (80% vs 50% of lecturers) and research assistants (53% vs 25%), but lecturers had larger overall groups, likely due to undergraduate students.
evaluation: The claims provide consistent data on group composition with specific percentages. The explanation for recruitment difficulties (doctoral training centers, student preferences) and larger lecturer groups (undergraduates) are reasonable inferences supported by the data patterns.

result: A spike in male appointments occurred in 2013 (47 men vs 21 women), likely due to recruitment before REF2014. This wave of appointments significantly favored male applicants, possibly due to increased head-hunting or informal recruitment practices. The gender gap has since narrowed (gap of 1 in 2017-2018).
evaluation: Claims C66, C70, C71, and C72 provide specific data on appointment patterns by year and gender. The explanation linking this to REF2014 (C67, C68, C123) is speculative but reasonable given the timing. The proposed mechanisms (C69, C124) are explicitly marked as speculation.

result: The survey was distributed through multiple channels (Twitter, email, LinkedIn, NewPI slack), with 311 of 365 respondents recruited via Twitter. The sample has similar gender and nationality breakdown to UK Higher Education Statistics Agency data for sciences.
evaluation: The claims clearly document the survey methodology and recruitment sources with specific numbers. The comparison to external statistics (C99) provides validation of sample representativeness, though the authors acknowledge this is not a fully representative sample.

result: The academic system trains more PhDs and postdocs than can be employed as PIs or lecturers, resulting in intense competition for these positions. New PIs face wide-ranging challenges in establishing research groups and undertaking new responsibilities.
evaluation: These claims describe well-established structural features of the academic system. While presented as general knowledge rather than survey findings, they provide important context for interpreting the survey results.

result: Despite only 4 respondents working part-time, flexible working is often suggested for work-life balance. Given the challenges facing new PIs, it is unsurprising that part-time work is rare, and other mechanisms are needed to improve work-life balance.
evaluation: The observation about part-time work rarity (C16, C108) is well-supported by data. The inference that other mechanisms are needed (C109) is reasonable given the documented work-life balance dissatisfaction, though C106 is a recommendation rather than a finding.
